analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer credit interest rates nationwide and limits fees lenders can charge to $15.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national usury limit into federal law: no lender could charge an interest rate more than 8 percentage points above a benchmark rate set by the Federal Reserve, and no fee or charge in a credit transaction could exceed $15. It also would have stopped credit card companies from using outside negative information on a credit report to raise a cardholder's interest rate when the cardholder's own account was in good standing. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry credit card balances and take out consumer loans. They would pay a capped interest rate instead of whatever rate the lender charges, pay no more than $15 in fees on a credit transaction, and would no longer face rate hikes triggered by negative information elsewhere in their credit file, such as a late payment on an unrelated account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders and consumer borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the annual percentage rate on any extension of credit at no more than 8 percentage points above a benchmark rate determined by the Federal Reserve, replacing a system where card issuers can charge any rate the market allows.
It caps any fee or charge a creditor may impose under the terms of a credit transaction at $15.

It prohibits a credit card issuer from using negative information in a consumer report to raise a card's interest rate, or to remove or raise an introductory rate, for reasons other than the cardholder's own actions on that account.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, banks, and other consumer lenders, who would lose the ability to charge uncapped interest rates and penalty fees, including the practice of raising rates based on unrelated credit report information.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: A hard national rate cap could shrink access to credit for borrowers with poor credit histories, since lenders who cannot price for higher risk may decline to lend to them at all, an objection supporters of such caps would need to answer.
The $15 fee cap applies to any fee or charge in any credit transaction, which could prevent lenders from recovering realistic costs of servicing riskier loans.
The interest cap is tied to a formula benchmark rather than a fixed number, so the ceiling would move with the benchmark rate set by the Federal Reserve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying revolving card debt at rates that can run well above 20%, a national rate ceiling and a $15 fee cap would mean direct, measurable savings. The real trade-off is access: capping rates and fees can make it uneconomical to lend to the riskiest borrowers, so some people might have fewer borrowing options even as borrowing gets cheaper for those who qualify. The bill does nothing to address how credit is extended to people the cap would price out, which is the strongest good-faith objection to it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, received no hearing or vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders introduced the Loan Shark Prevention Act in the House on April 13, 2005, with 19 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, and on May 19, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
Twenty-four members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, but no further action was taken and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders kept the ability to charge uncapped interest rates and fees, and cardholders continued paying those rates and fees. The members of the Financial Services Committee were never required to take a position on the record.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on April 13, 2005.

for.name: 24 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 24 were Democrats, including Reps. Weiner, Conyers, Kucinich, George Miller, Stark, Cummings, and Schakowsky.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and members of the House Financial Services Committee, 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill remained parked in the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit from May 2005 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an independent who aligned with Democrats, and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats; no vote was ever taken, so no cross-party record exists.

industries.note: The bill would cap the interest rates and fees that are the core of card issuer revenue, and would bar rate increases triggered by credit report information unrelated to the cardholder's account. Lenders' interest in keeping rates and fees uncapped runs directly against borrowers' interest in paying less. [S3]
A national usury ceiling applies to any extension of credit, not just credit cards, so high-rate consumer lenders would lose the ability to charge rates above the cap. [S3]
